verdict: build the collector, buy nothing, and keep the publisher deliberately small
why: Two halves with opposite answers, which is why this is one record and not two. The COLLECTOR half is unbuyable off the shelf for a reason that has nothing to do with capability: every observability product ingests events an application emits through its SDK, and this repository emits nothing. What it has is ten append-only JSONL ledgers written by hooks, each with a different schema (bus.jsonl stamps `ts` and identifies as `from_lane`; claims.jsonl uses `claimed_at` and `lane`; handback-log.jsonl has only action/reason/session/ts and no lane at all). Adopting Langfuse or an OTel collector means instrumenting ten hook scripts to emit spans, which is strictly more work than reading the files they already write, and it adds a service that must be running for telemetry to exist. The PUBLISHER half is the opposite: GitHub Issues is entirely off-the-shelf and this file is a thin `gh issue comment` wrapper on purpose, 202 lines of which the API call is one.

alternatives.name: tools/bus/bus.py, already in this repo
alternatives.covers: The message transport, completely, and better than anything here would. It is hash-chained, lane-derived-from-cwd, has per-lane read cursors, and is ALREADY WIRED to two live hooks (SessionStart and UserPromptSubmit both run `bus.py inbox`). It is not superseded and must not be. What it does not solve is the reason it holds 25 messages with none since 2026-07-30: reading was automatic from the start and SENDING is voluntary. This component addresses the sending side by deriving messages from ledgers, and its natural next step is to emit bus rows rather than only GitHub comments.

alternatives.name: Langfuse / LangSmith / W&B Weave
alternatives.covers: The collector half and far more: tracing, evals, cost attribution, a UI. Rejected on the ingestion boundary, not on features. All three want the agent to emit through their SDK, and the agent here is Claude Code, whose hooks write JSONL and cannot be made to emit spans without rewriting them. Self-hosted Langfuse also needs Postgres and a running server, against a repo whose whole tooling convention is stdlib-only files with no daemon. Revisit if a hook is ever rewritten to emit structured spans, at which point the ingestion objection disappears.

alternatives.name: OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions
alternatives.covers: The event SCHEMA, and this is the alternative most likely to win at recheck. The normalised shape here (ts, repo, lane, source, kind, severity, subject, ref) is an ad-hoc schema where a standard one exists. It was not adopted now because the semconv is still evolving and mapping a `claims.jsonl` row onto a span is a poor fit, but if this stream ever needs to leave the machine for anything other than a GitHub comment, adopting the convention beats keeping a private schema.

alternatives.name: Slack, Discord, or a real chat product
alternatives.covers: The comms half properly, with presence, threads, search and mobile. Excluded by the operator's own framing ('like slack but without slack') and by one structural fact: a chat product is a separate identity and permission system, while the agents here already authenticate to GitHub and already work in issues. The feature actually wanted from Slack is the notification, and a GitHub issue comment delivers exactly that.

alternatives.name: GitHub Actions workflow summaries, or a job that posts the ledger
alternatives.covers: A plausible zero-new-code option: let CI publish. Rejected because most of these events happen on the local machine and never reach CI. 6613 of 7029 gate rows are local selftest fixtures and the real local runs outnumber the CI ones; a CI-only publisher would report the small half.

alternatives.name: do nothing, keep reading state/ by hand
alternatives.covers: The honest baseline, and it loses on a measured fact rather than a preference. The ledgers are local to one machine and one directory: every hook writes to `$CLAUDE_OS_DIR` defaulting to `~/claude-setup`, so a session working in new-recruit lands its rows in claude-setup and nothing in new-recruit can see them. Reading by hand also does not scale past the volume: the first dry run produced 25 alerts of which 23 were selftest fixtures.

evidence: Built and run this session, not designed on paper. (1) Ledger schemas were read from a real last row of each of the ten files before any extractor was written; the audit table (`collect.py --audit`) reports rows, events and skipped lines per source, and the selftest asserts a nonzero yield PER SOURCE rather than in total, because a healthy total hides one silent ledger. Current yield: 9 sources, 8822 events, 0 skipped lines. (2) The repo-attribution defect was found by running it: attributing a row to the directory holding the file labelled all 8822 events `claude-setup`, because every hook writes to a fixed path. Corrected to prefer the row's own repo/project/project_path/cwd, and the cross-repo view then resolved to claude-setup 1906, new-recruit 173, daily-deep-learning 82, moneyballz 11, with an `origin` field recording which attribution was used (6916 row-derived, 1906 file-location). (3) The fixture-flood defect was found by the first `publish.py --dry-run`, whose output was 23 of 25 lines of `gate FAIL on tmpd1fy6797` from the gate's own selftest; measured at 6613 of 7029 gate rows. Filtered on project_path being under a temp root rather than on a `tmp` name prefix, and DOWNGRADED to trace rather than dropped so the ratio stays measurable. After the fix the same dry run surfaces a real cross-repo alert, `gate FAIL on new-recruit: unit, types`, which was previously buried. (4) Both selftests pass offline with no network and no credential: collect 6 checks, publish 7. (5) The publisher's safety property is verified by parsing its own source for the `args.post and args.issue` conjunction, because a test that actually posted would defeat the property it verifies. (6) LIVE 2026-08-04: operator approved publishing. Issue #38 created, first batch of 25 items posted (comment 5183809359), cursor advanced to 24 fingerprints. Deduplication proved by re-running immediately: the second selection is entirely DIFFERENT events (older refutations) with 12 further items of backlog reported, not the same 25 again. A systemd user timer (agent-feed.timer, OnUnitActiveSec=30min, Persistent=true) is enabled and its next elapse is scheduled; the service ran once on demand and correctly printed 'throttled: last post was 1.2 min ago, floor is 30'. Units are versioned at tools/telemetry/systemd/.
recheck: Run all five; any one flipping re-opens the verdict. (1) Is the feed still read? `gh issue view <n> --comments` and count reactions or replies. If the feed has posts and no engagement, it has become the bus's successor in the worst way and the answer is to post less, not more. (2) Did the derived-not-composed property hold? Grep the publisher for any code path that takes free text from an agent. (3) Has an agent hook been rewritten to emit structured spans? If so, re-evaluate Langfuse and the OTel GenAI semconv, because the ingestion objection that excluded them will have disappeared. (4) Is the fixture filter still accurate? `collect.py --audit` plus a count of gate rows whose project_path is under a temp root; a change in how gate.py builds fixtures could make the filter over- or under-match. (5) WebSearch "agent telemetry github issues bus" and "claude code hooks observability" for a maintained tool that ingests JSONL directly rather than through an SDK.
what_ours_does: collect.py normalises ten heterogeneous state/ ledgers across every repo under ~/work/repos into one severity-graded event stream, attributing each row to the repo it is ABOUT rather than the directory it sits in, and reports per-source yield so a silently-empty ledger cannot masquerade as a quiet period. publish.py selects only alert- and note-level events, deduplicates them by a timestamp-independent fingerprint so the same fact never posts twice, caps the volume and states what it dropped, and comments them onto an existing GitHub issue that acts as the agent feed. Nothing posts without both --post and an explicit --issue, no issue is ever created, and the cursor advances only on a successful post.
strongest_counterargument: The feed now exists and is fed, which proves the machinery and not the premise. The bet is that deriving messages beats asking an agent to send them, and the only evidence that will settle it is whether anything ever ACTS on a feed item. This repo has now built three message surfaces and used one of them 25 times in ten days. A second and sharper objection: the timer runs on a WSL instance that only exists while a terminal is open, so 'independent of session activity' is true of sessions and false of the machine. If the operator closes WSL overnight, the feed is as session-bound as the thing it replaced, and Persistent=true only buys one catch-up run.
